2	//
3	// Why any of this exists at serve time rather than purely in generation:
4	// the builder prompt is told to fill in index.html's <head>, but a prompt is
5	// guidance, not a guarantee. Everything here is a backstop that runs on the
6	// way out, so a site can never be published with the foundation's placeholder
7	// title — which is exactly what shipped before (every site was "Kodely Site",
8	// in the browser tab, in Google, and in every link preview).
9	//
10	// It also fixes ALREADY-published sites with no regeneration, because it
11	// rewrites on read rather than at build time.

13	const SITES_BASE = process.env.KODELY_SITES_BASE ?? "kodely.site";
14	
15	// The foundation's placeholder. If this survives to serve time the agent
16	// didn't personalise the head, so we substitute the real project name.
17	const PLACEHOLDER_TITLE = "Kodely Site";

19	/**
20	 * Public base URL of a published site, as a visitor sees it.
21	 *
22	 * Two shapes, because the proxy rewrites the branded subdomain onto an
23	 * internal path:
24	 *   <slug>.kodely.site/         -> internally /api/site/<slug>
25	 *   staging.kodely.me/api/site/<slug>/   (no wildcard DNS off prod)
26	 *
27	 * Canonical/OG URLs must use the EXTERNAL form or they point somewhere the
28	 * visitor's browser never went, so this keys off the Host header.
29	 */
30	export function siteBaseUrl(req: Request, slug: string): string {
31	  const host = req.headers.get("host") ?? "";
32	  const bare = host.split(":")[0];
33	
34	  // Deliberately NOT derived from x-forwarded-proto. Cloudflare's SSL mode
35	  // here is Flexible: it terminates TLS at the edge and talks to the origin
36	  // over plain HTTP, so nginx forwards `x-forwarded-proto: http` even though
37	  // the visitor is on https. Trusting it emitted http:// canonical and og:url
38	  // on sites that are only reachable over https.
39	  //
40	  // That was invisible in testing because Cloudflare's Automatic HTTPS
41	  // Rewrites silently repairs href="http://..." (canonical) but NOT
42	  // content="http://..." (og:url) — so only the OG tag stayed wrong, and
43	  // only when checked through the real edge.
44	  //
45	  // Every published site is reachable only via the Cloudflare HTTPS edge, so
46	  // anything that isn't loopback is https by definition.
47	  const isLocal = bare === "localhost" || bare === "127.0.0.1" || bare === "::1";
48	  const proto = isLocal ? "http" : "https";
49	  // Branded subdomain: the site lives at the host root.
50	  if (bare.endsWith(`.${SITES_BASE}`)) return `${proto}://${host}`;
51	  // Otherwise it is served under a path (staging, localhost).
52	  return `${proto}://${host}/api/site/${slug}`;
53	}

55	/**
56	 * The public URL of ONE built HTML file — the single definition of a page's
57	 * address.
58	 *
59	 * Sites are multi-page now (see lib/foundation.ts): `vite build` emits one real
60	 * document per page, and the site route serves `about.html` for a request to
61	 * `/about`. Three things have to agree on what a page's address IS — its
62	 * <link rel="canonical">, its og:url, and its <loc> in sitemap.xml — and they
63	 * agree by all coming from here. A sitemap advertising /about while the page at
64	 * /about canonicalises elsewhere is a self-cancelling instruction: Google drops
65	 * the URL rather than guessing which half to believe.
66	 *
67	 * Extensionless is the canonical form, so /about and /about.html — the route
68	 * answers both — collapse onto one indexable URL instead of competing as two.
69	 */
70	export function pageUrl(baseUrl: string, htmlPath: string): string {
71	  return baseUrl.replace(/\/$/, "") + pagePath(htmlPath);
72	}
73	
74	/** "index.html" -> "", "about.html" -> "/about", "blog/index.html" -> "/blog". */
75	function pagePath(htmlPath: string): string {
76	  const stripped = htmlPath
77	    .replace(/^\/+/, "")
78	    .replace(/\.html?$/i, "")
79	    // A directory index IS the directory: blog/index.html is /blog, and a bare
80	    // index at the root is the site root itself.
81	    .replace(/(^|\/)index$/i, "$1")
82	    .replace(/\/+$/, "");
83	  return stripped ? `/${stripped}` : "";
84	}
85	
86	function escapeHtml(s: string): string {
87	  return s
88	    .replace(/&/g, "&")
89	    .replace(/</g, "<")
90	    .replace(/>/g, ">")
91	    .replace(/"/g, """);
92	}
93	
94	function escapeXml(s: string): string {
95	  return escapeHtml(s).replace(/'/g, "'");
96	}
97	
98	/**
99	 * Undo the entity encoding in text pulled back OUT of the HTML.
100	 *
101	 * The title is read from inside <title>…</title>, where it is already encoded —
102	 * a site called "Bloom & Co" is stored as "Bloom & Co". Composing the
103	 * fallback description from that string and then escaping it again produced
104	 * "Bloom &amp; Co", and the literal entity showed up in every link preview.
105	 * Decoding first, then escaping once, is the round trip that holds.
106	 *
107	 * Only the five entities escapeHtml/escapeXml can produce. A general HTML
108	 * entity decoder is not wanted here: this exists purely to invert our own
109	 * escaping, and anything else the builder wrote should pass through untouched.
110	 */
111	function decodeHtml(s: string): string {
112	  return s
113	    .replace(/</g, "<")
114	    .replace(/>/g, ">")
115	    .replace(/"/g, '"')
116	    .replace(/'/g, "'")
117	    // Ampersand LAST, so "&lt;" decodes to "<" rather than "<".
118	    .replace(/&/g, "&");
119	}
120	
121	/** Absolutise a root-relative URL against the site's public base. */
122	function absolutise(value: string, base: string): string {
123	  if (/^https?:\/\//i.test(value) || value.startsWith("data:")) return value;
124	  return `${base.replace(/\/$/, "")}/${value.replace(/^\//, "")}`;
125	}
126	
127	/**
128	 * Ensure a served HTML document has a real title, a description, canonical
129	 * and OG/Twitter tags. Only fills gaps — anything the builder already wrote
130	 * is left exactly as-is, since it had the site's actual content in view and
131	 * this function does not.
132	 */
133	export function applySeo(
134	  html: string,
135	  opts: {
136	    projectName: string;
137	    baseUrl: string;
138	    /**
139	     * This page's own URL, from pageUrl() — what canonical and og:url describe.
140	     *
141	     * MULTI-PAGE DEPENDS ON THIS. Both used to be `baseUrl`, which was correct
142	     * while every site was one page and actively harmful the moment one is not:
143	     * every subpage would have declared the HOME PAGE as its canonical, which
144	     * is not a hint, it is an instruction to drop /about, /services and /contact
145	     * from the index entirely. Multi-page exists FOR the extra indexable pages,
146	     * so shipping it without this would have shipped the opposite of the point.
147	     *
148	     * Defaults to baseUrl, which is the right answer for a single-page site.
149	     */
150	    pageUrl?: string;
151	  },
152	): string {
153	  const { projectName, baseUrl } = opts;
154	  const selfUrl = opts.pageUrl ?? baseUrl;
155	  if (!/<head[\s>]/i.test(html)) return html; // not a full document; leave alone
156	
157	  let out = html;
158	
159	  // 1. Title — replace the placeholder, or add one if missing entirely.
160	  const titleMatch = out.match(/<title>([\s\S]*?)<\/title>/i);
161	  const currentTitle = titleMatch?.[1]?.trim();
162	  const title = !currentTitle || currentTitle === PLACEHOLDER_TITLE ? projectName : currentTitle;
163	  // Replacements go through FUNCTIONS, never strings. In a string replacement
164	  // `$` is a substitution sigil — `$&`, `` $` ``, `$'` and `$1` are expanded,
165	  // and escapeHtml does not escape `$`. A project called "Everything $1 Store"
166	  // silently lost the `$1`, and a value containing `` $` `` spliced the entire
167	  // preceding document into the tag. applySeo runs on every read of every
168	  // published site, so this was live on the serving path.
169	  if (titleMatch) {
170	    if (currentTitle !== title) {
171	      out = out.replace(/<title>[\s\S]*?<\/title>/i, () => `<title>${escapeHtml(title)}</title>`);
172	    }
173	  } else {
174	    out = out.replace(
175	      /<head([^>]*)>/i,
176	      (_m, attrs: string) => `<head${attrs}>\n    <title>${escapeHtml(title)}</title>`,
177	    );
178	  }
179	
180	  const inject: string[] = [];
181	
182	  // Upsert a <meta>/<link>: fill it when the tag is absent OR present with an
183	  // empty value. The foundation ships empty `content=""` scaffolding to show
184	  // the builder what to write, so "tag exists" alone is not good enough — an
185	  // existence-only check would leave those empty forever.
186	  const upsert = (attrRe: RegExp, valueAttr: "content" | "href", value: string, tag: string) => {
187	    const existing = out.match(attrRe);
188	    if (!existing) {
189	      inject.push(tag);
190	      return;
191	    }
192	    const valRe = new RegExp(`${valueAttr}=["']([^"']*)["']`, "i");
193	    const current = existing[0].match(valRe)?.[1];
194	    if (current === undefined || current.trim() === "") {
195	      // Replacer function, not a string — see the note above the title block.
196	      out = out.replace(existing[0], () => tag);
197	    }
198	  };
199	
200	  // decodeHtml first: `title` may have come straight out of <title>…</title>,
201	  // where it is already escaped. Without this, escapeHtml below double-encodes
202	  // it and the raw entity is what people see in the link preview.
203	  const desc = `${decodeHtml(title)} — built with Kodely.`;
204	  upsert(
205	    /<meta\s+name=["']description["'][^>]*>/i,
206	    "content",
207	    desc,
208	    `<meta name="description" content="${escapeHtml(desc)}" />`,
209	  );
210	  upsert(
211	    /<link\s+rel=["']canonical["'][^>]*>/i,
212	    "href",
213	    selfUrl,
214	    `<link rel="canonical" href="${escapeHtml(selfUrl)}" />`,
215	  );
216	  // decodeHtml for the same reason as `desc` above, and this one matters more:
217	  // og:title is the line a link preview shows first. `title` may have come
218	  // straight out of <title>…</title> already escaped, so escaping it again
219	  // rendered "Bloom & Co" as "Bloom & Co" in every share card. The earlier
220	  // fix covered `desc` and missed this — caught by tests/site-seo.test.mjs.
221	  upsert(
222	    /<meta\s+property=["']og:title["'][^>]*>/i,
223	    "content",
224	    title,
225	    `<meta property="og:title" content="${escapeHtml(decodeHtml(title))}" />`,
226	  );
227	  upsert(
228	    /<meta\s+property=["']og:description["'][^>]*>/i,
229	    "content",
230	    desc,
231	    `<meta property="og:description" content="${escapeHtml(desc)}" />`,
232	  );
233	  upsert(
234	    /<meta\s+property=["']og:type["'][^>]*>/i,
235	    "content",
236	    "website",
237	    `<meta property="og:type" content="website" />`,
238	  );
239	  upsert(
240	    /<meta\s+property=["']og:url["'][^>]*>/i,
241	    "content",
242	    selfUrl,
243	    `<meta property="og:url" content="${escapeHtml(selfUrl)}" />`,
244	  );
245	  upsert(
246	    /<meta\s+name=["']twitter:card["'][^>]*>/i,
247	    "content",
248	    "summary_large_image",
249	    `<meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image" />`,
250	  );
251	
252	  if (inject.length) {
253	    out = out.replace(/<\/head>/i, `  ${inject.join("\n    ")}\n  </head>`);
254	  }
255	
256	  // Crawlers reject relative og:image, so absolutise whatever the builder set.
257	  out = out.replace(
258	    /(<meta\s+property=["']og:image["']\s+content=["'])([^"']+)(["'])/gi,
259	    (_m, pre, url, post) => `${pre}${escapeHtml(absolutise(url, baseUrl))}${post}`,
260	  );
261	
262	  return out;
263	}

265	/** robots.txt pointing crawlers at the sitemap. Generated, never stored. */
266	export function robotsTxt(baseUrl: string): string {
267	  return `User-agent: *\nAllow: /\n\nSitemap: ${baseUrl.replace(/\/$/, "")}/sitemap.xml\n`;
268	}

270	/**
271	 * sitemap.xml from the site's published HTML files — ONE ENTRY PER PAGE.
272	 * Generated per request so it can use the visitor-facing host and can never
273	 * drift from what is served.
274	 *
275	 * Every loc goes through pageUrl(), which is also what stamps each page's
276	 * canonical tag, so the sitemap and the pages it lists cannot disagree. It is
277	 * also what makes the dedupe real rather than cosmetic: about.html and
278	 * /about.html were already collapsed, but so are about.html and about/index.html
279	 * — two files that would otherwise have listed the same page twice.
280	 */
281	export function sitemapXml(baseUrl: string, htmlPaths: string[], lastMod?: Date): string {
282	  const seen = new Set<string>();
283	  const urls = htmlPaths
284	    .map((p) => pageUrl(baseUrl, p))
285	    .filter((u) => (seen.has(u) ? false : (seen.add(u), true)))
286	    .map((u) => {
287	      const loc = escapeXml(u);
288	      const mod = lastMod ? `\n    <lastmod>${lastMod.toISOString().slice(0, 10)}</lastmod>` : "";
289	      return `  <url>\n    <loc>${loc}</loc>${mod}\n  </url>`;
290	    })
291	    .join("\n");
292	  return `<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>\n<urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9">\n${urls}\n</urlset>\n`;
293	}

104	  return [`${clean}.html`, `${clean}/index.html`];
105	}
106	
107	/**
108	 * The only POST shapes a published site's own origin ever answers:
109	 *
110	 *  - `/__forms/<formName>`, which arrives here as
111	 *    `/api/site/<slug>/__forms/<formName>` via proxy.ts. Everything — host
112	 *    check, published check, caps, abuse control, storage and the owner
113	 *    notification — is in lib/site-forms.ts.
114	 *  - `/__records/<kind>`, the generic storage primitive behind
115	 *    backend-backed site features (bookings, client portals, simple data —
116	 *    see lib/site-records.ts). Same shape, same safety machinery, no
117	 *    product-specific logic here or there.
118	 *  - `/__records/<kind>/<id>`, the update/cancel target for the "manage
119	 *    this" link `/__records/<kind>` handed the submitter — one path segment
120	 *    longer, dispatched separately because it needs a token, not an origin
121	 *    check alone.
122	 *  - `/__auth/request` and `/__auth/logout` — the magic-link visitor-account
123	 *    system (see lib/site-auth.ts): asking for a sign-in link, and signing
124	 *    out. `/__auth/verify` (the link itself) is a GET, dispatched below.
125	 *
126	 * Anything that is not one of these exact path shapes is a 404 in the
127	 * handler it's dispatched to, so this does not become a general POST surface
128	 * on the sites domain.
129	 */
130	export async function POST(
131	  req: Request,
132	  { params }: { params: Promise<{ slug: string; path?: string[] }> },
133	) {
134	  const { slug, path } = await params;
135	  const segments = path ?? [];
136	  if (segments[0] === RECORD_PATH_SEGMENT) {
137	    return segments.length === 3
138	      ? submitSiteRecordUpdate(req, slug, segments)
139	      : submitSiteRecord(req, slug, segments);
140	  }
141	  if (segments[0] === AUTH_PATH_SEGMENT) {
142	    if (segments[1] === "request") return requestSiteLogin(req, slug, segments);
143	    if (segments[1] === "logout") return logoutSiteVisitor(req, slug, segments);
144	    return siteNotFound();
145	  }
146	  return submitSiteForm(req, slug, segments);
147	}
148	
149	export async function GET(
150	  req: Request,
151	  { params }: { params: Promise<{ slug: string; path?: string[] }> },
152	) {
153	  const { slug, path } = await params;
154	  const filePath = path && path.length > 0 ? path.join("/") : "index.html";
155	
156	  // Generated pages are only ever first-party to the sites domain. proxy.ts
157	  // turns this request away earlier for the same reason, but a route handler
158	  // must not depend on that: the proxy's own matcher can miss paths, and the
159	  // proxy is explicit (see its header comment) that it is never the only gate.
160	  //
161	  // The response is byte-identical to the "no such site" 404 below, so it does
162	  // not confirm that a slug exists to someone probing the wrong host.
163	  if (!siteHostAllowed(req.headers.get("host") ?? "", slug)) {
164	    return new Response("Site not found.", { status: 404 });
165	  }
166	
167	  // `/__records/<kind>/<id>` — the "manage this" link handed out by
168	  // lib/site-records.ts's create reply. Dispatched here, before the file
169	  // lookup below, because it is not a stored file at all; everything about
170	  // it (host check, token check, the invalid-link reply) lives in
171	  // lib/site-records.ts, same division of labour as the POST dispatch above.
172	  if (path && path.length === 3 && path[0] === RECORD_PATH_SEGMENT) {
173	    return viewSiteRecord(req, slug, path);
174	  }
175	
176	  // `/__auth/verify` — the magic-link visitor-account system's own GET route
177	  // (lib/site-auth.ts). Same reasoning as the manage-link dispatch above: not
178	  // a stored file, dispatched before the file lookup.
179	  if (path && path.length === 2 && path[0] === AUTH_PATH_SEGMENT && path[1] === "verify") {
180	    return verifySiteLogin(req, slug, path);
181	  }
182	
183	  const project = await db.project.findUnique({ where: { slug } });
184	  if (!project || !project.publishedAt) {
185	    return new Response("Site not found.", { status: 404 });
186	  }
187	
188	  const baseUrl = siteBaseUrl(req, slug);
189	  const seoHeaders = {
190	    "Content-Security-Policy": SANDBOX_CSP,
191	    "Cache-Control": "public, max-age=60",
192	  };
193	
194	  // robots.txt and sitemap.xml are generated, not stored — they depend on the
195	  // visitor-facing host (which differs between the branded subdomain and the
196	  // staging path form), so a file baked at build time would be wrong on one of
197	  // them. A site that ships its own copy still wins: we only synthesise these
198	  // when the project has no such file.
199	  if (filePath === "robots.txt" || filePath === "sitemap.xml") {
200	    const own = await db.projectFile.findFirst({
201	      where: { projectId: project.id, path: filePath, published: true, kind: "build" },
202	    });
203	    if (!own) {
204	      if (filePath === "robots.txt") {
205	        return new Response(robotsTxt(baseUrl), {
206	          headers: { ...seoHeaders, "Content-Type": MIME.txt },
207	        });
208	      }
209	      const pages = await db.projectFile.findMany({
210	        where: { projectId: project.id, published: true, kind: "build", path: { endsWith: ".html" } },
211	        select: { path: true },
212	      });
213	      return new Response(
214	        sitemapXml(baseUrl, pages.map((p) => p.path), project.publishedAt ?? undefined),
215	        { headers: { ...seoHeaders, "Content-Type": MIME.xml } },
216	      );
217	    }
218	  }
219	
220	  // One query for both spellings of a page, then the caller's preference order
221	  // decides — /about must not cost two round trips to answer.
222	  const candidates = candidatePaths(filePath);
223	  const matches = await db.projectFile.findMany({
224	    where: { projectId: project.id, path: { in: candidates }, published: true, kind: "build" },
225	  });
226	  const file = candidates.map((c) => matches.find((m) => m.path === c)).find(Boolean);
227	  if (!file) {
228	    return new Response("Not found.", { status: 404 });
229	  }
230	
231	  const ext = file.path.split(".").pop() ?? "";
232	
233	  // Backstop so no site can ship with the foundation's placeholder <title>.
234	  // Only fills gaps — anything the builder wrote itself is preserved.
235	  //
236	  // pageUrl(), not baseUrl: canonical and og:url must name THIS page. Keyed off
237	  // the file that actually answered, so /about and /about.html both canonicalise
238	  // to /about and Google sees one page rather than two competing duplicates.
239	  // Live read-back (Phase 1B): a builder-authored `data-kodely-records="<kind>"`
240	  // container gets its matching SiteRecord rows rendered into it, server-side,
241	  // per request — see lib/site-record-render.ts. Runs BEFORE applySeo() only
242	  // because there is no ordering dependency between the two and this keeps
243	  // "content" and "head metadata" as two separate passes over the string,
244	  // each easy to reason about alone; applySeo() never looks at anything this
245	  // step could have touched (it only touches <head>).
246	  //
247	  // `data-kodely-mine` (Phase 2) needs to know who is currently signed in —
248	  // resolveSiteVisitor() is the SAME cookie/hash/lookup lib/site-auth.ts's
249	  // record-creation path uses, so the two can never disagree about what
250	  // "signed in" means. Only resolved when the page actually uses the
251	  // attribute, so an ordinary page pays no extra query for a feature it
252	  // doesn't use.
253	  const visitorId =
254	    ext === "html" && file.content.includes("data-kodely-mine")
255	      ? ((await resolveSiteVisitor(req, project.id))?.id ?? null)
256	      : null;
257	
258	  const body =
259	    ext === "html"
260	      ? applySeo(await renderSiteRecords(file.content, project.id, visitorId), {
261	          projectName: project.name,
262	          baseUrl,
263	          pageUrl: pageUrl(baseUrl, file.path),
264	        })
265	      : file.content;
266	
267	  return new Response(body, {
268	    headers: { ...seoHeaders, "Content-Type": MIME[ext] ?? "application/octet-stream" },
269	  });
270	}

1	/**
2	 * Starter prompts for the gallery at /templates.
3	 *
4	 * The prompt is the product here, not the card. Each one is written the way an
5	 * expert user would write it — audience, purpose, tone, the sections wanted,
6	 * and bracketed placeholders for the facts only the owner knows.
7	 *
8	 * Every prompt is written to stay inside what a generated site actually IS
9	 * (see the SYSTEM prompt in lib/agent.ts and the starting files in
10	 * lib/foundation.ts): one Vite + React + TS + Tailwind page, served under a
11	 * CSP that blocks every external host, with no backend — EXCEPT the one real
12	 * exception documented in lib/agent.ts and lib/site-forms.ts: a plain HTML
13	 * contact form posting to the site's own `/__forms/<name>` genuinely works,
14	 * is stored, and emails the owner. So no template may ask for — or imply — a
15	 * working booking form, an account, a cart, a database, a live API call, a
16	 * remote or stock image, a custom web font, or a second page. A contact form
17	 * IS fair game where the brief calls for one.
18	 *
19	 * The 23 prompts below predate that exception and were written when contact
20	 * forms were also refused — most say "no backend, use mailto:" in the same
21	 * breath as booking/checkout. That is still correct for booking, checkout,
22	 * accounts and search; it is now OVERLY CAUTIOUS about plain contact. See the
23	 * board for the follow-up to revise each one individually — a vertical like
24	 * legal or trades wants the real contact form, not just a mailto: link.
25	 *
26	 * Where a vertical normally leans on something that still cannot work
27	 * (bookings, RSVPs, donations, checkout, waitlists), the prompt asks for a
28	 * link-out instead — a mailto:, a tel:, or a clearly-bracketed [link to your
29	 * …] — and the card's own description says so, so nobody clicks expecting a
30	 * booking system.
31	 *
32	 * Two agent rules the prompts are written to cooperate with rather than
33	 * fight: never invent facts about a real business (hence the brackets), and
34	 * never build a control that only pretends to work (hence the link-outs).
35	 */
36	
37	export const TEMPLATE_CATEGORIES = [
38	  "Food & drink",
39	  "Beauty & wellness",
40	  "Local services",
41	  "Professional services",
42	  "Personal & creative",
43	  "Startup & product",
44	  "Events & causes",
45	] as const;
46	
47	export type TemplateCategory = (typeof TEMPLATE_CATEGORIES)[number];
48	
49	export type Template = {
50	  /** Stable — it ends up in URLs and analytics, so never renumber these. */
51	  id: string;
52	  name: string;
53	  /**
54	   * One honest sentence. If the vertical usually implies a backend feature
55	   * this can't deliver, that limit belongs HERE, not in the small print.
56	   */
57	  description: string;
58	  category: TemplateCategory;
59	  /** The full starter prompt — exactly what lands in the composer. */
60	  prompt: string;
61	};
62	
63	export const TEMPLATES: Template[] = [
64	  // ---------------------------------------------------------------- Food
65	  {
66	    id: "restaurant",
67	    name: "Restaurant",
68	    description:
69	      "A one-page site with menu highlights, hours and location. Bookings link out to your phone or existing reservation service — there is no built-in reservation system.",
70	    category: "Food & drink",
71	    prompt: `Build a one-page website for [your restaurant's name], a [cuisine, e.g. modern Italian] restaurant in [your city].
72	
73	Audience: locals deciding where to eat tonight, plus people who were recommended us and want to check we look good before calling. Tone: warm and appetising, confident, never corporate.
74	
75	Sections in this order:
76	1. Hero — the name, a single line describing the food, and a "Call to book" button.
77	2. A short paragraph about the kitchen: what we cook, where the ingredients come from, why it tastes the way it does.
78	3. Menu highlights — 6 to 8 dishes grouped as starters / mains / desserts, each with a one-line description and a price.
79	4. Hours and location, laid out so they are readable at a glance.
80	5. A footer with social links.
81	
82	Leave every fact you cannot know as an obvious bracketed placeholder for me to fill in — [your address], [your phone number], [your opening hours], dish names and prices — instead of inventing something plausible.
83

## Findings

**1. `lib/agent.ts` — the multi-page prompt guidance**

The system prompt's "Multi-page" section (lines ~51–57) is genuinely rigorous, not a throwaway mention:
- Spells out the exact 3-file recipe for adding a page: `src/pages/About.tsx`, an entry in `src/pages.tsx` (`{ path, label, component, nav? }`), and `about.html` at project root with its own `data-page`, `<title>`, description and OG tags.
- Explicitly warns "Skip step 3 and the page does not exist" and explains *why* per-page `<head>` matters (SEO — a shared title/description across pages competes with itself).
- Tells the model to link via `<Link to="/about">` from `src/router.tsx`, never a bare `<a href>`, and explains `SiteNav` self-builds from the page table.
- Gives real judgment guidance on *when* to use pages ("content genuinely differs... Don't manufacture thin pages to look bigger") rather than blindly multiplying pages.
- **Gap**: it documents *adding* a page in detail but has no analogous instructions for *removing* one (no "delete the .html shell, drop the pages.tsx entry, delete the orphaned component" checklist).

**2. `lib/foundation.ts` / `lib/build-site.ts` — is this a first-class shape?**

Yes, genuinely first-class, not a fragile edge case:
- `src/router.tsx` is a real ~40-line hand-rolled router (`PageDef`, `resolvePage`, `href`/`Link`, `navPages`) deliberately built without client-side routing (real document loads, not pushState) so back-button/SEO/preview-iframe all stay simple and correct.
- `src/pages.tsx` is a real, explicit page table (`PAGES: PageDef[]`), separate from the router mechanism by design.
- `SiteNav.tsx` derives its links from `navPages()` — adding an entry to the table alone updates nav everywhere, and it self-hides for one-page sites (`pages.length < 2`).
- `vite.config.ts` in the foundation **discovers** pages by scanning for `.html` files at build time (recursive, depth-capped) and turns each into a Rollup multi-entry — this is exactly why multi-page works with zero config changes even though the agent is barred from touching `vite.config.ts` (that file is `isProtectedPath`). This is a deliberate, well-reasoned design, not an accident.
- All pages share one `/src/main.tsx` bundle (one JS chunk), which the code comments explain is intentional for both cross-page cache reuse and compatibility with the editor's `srcdoc` preview.

**3. `lib/site-seo.ts` — sitemap completeness**

Sitemap generation genuinely enumerates every page and is unlikely to miss one, because it's driven by the actual served artifacts, not by the page table:
- `sitemapXml()` is built from `db.projectFile` rows of `kind: "build"` filtered by `path.endsWith(".html")` — i.e., every HTML file the last Vite build actually emitted, queried fresh per-request (not cached/stale).
- `pageUrl()`/`pagePath()` normalize `about.html` → `/about`, `blog/index.html` → `/blog`, and the sitemap dedupes so two spellings of the same page (`about.html` vs `about/index.html`) collapse to one `<loc>`.
- Canonical/`og:url` tags are stamped per-page via the same `pageUrl()` function the sitemap uses (`applySeo({ pageUrl: pageUrl(baseUrl, file.path) })`), so a page's own canonical and its sitemap entry cannot disagree — this is explicitly tested (`tests/site-seo.test.mjs`, e.g. "a subpage canonicalises to ITSELF, not to the home page", "one entry per page, for a real multi-page site").
- Caveat: since the sitemap enumerates *built* HTML files rather than `pages.tsx` entries, an orphaned `.html` file (still on disk/build output but no longer in the nav table) would still be listed — see point 6.

**4. `app/api/site/[slug]/[[...path]]/route.ts` — path resolution**

Re-verified: `candidatePaths()` correctly handles nested, arbitrary-depth paths, not just flat one level:
- Anything with an extension resolves to itself only (protects `/assets/*`, `robots.txt`, etc.).
- Otherwise it tries `${clean}.html` then `${clean}/index.html`, and `clean` is just the raw joined path — so `/services/plumbing` → tries `services/plumbing.html` then `services/plumbing/index.html`, with no depth limit. This is confirmed to work for nested pages, matching the `vite.config.ts` scanner's own recursive discovery (capped at depth 4, "a site is not nested deeper than this").
- Deliberately not an SPA catch-all — unknown paths 404 rather than soft-404ing to the homepage, which is a correct SEO decision but also means a *broken* nav link (see point 6) will produce a real 404, not silently paper over the mistake.

**5. Customer-facing UI — the real gap**

This is where the story changes. Grepping `InlineWizard.tsx`, `TemplatePickerModal.tsx`, and `lib/templates.ts` for "multi-page"/"multi page"/"second page" returns **zero hits**. Concretely:
- **`lib/templates.ts`**: the file's own top-of-file doc comment states the constraint every one of the 23 templates is written to satisfy: sites must stay "one Vite + React + TS + Tailwind page... no backend... **no second page**." Every single template prompt literally opens with `"Build a one-page website for..."`.
- **`lib/wizard.ts`**: the generic skeleton and the `openingLine()` assembly function used by `InlineWizard` hardcode `"Build a one-page website for [name] — <description>."` as the very first sentence sent to the model — every time, regardless of what the customer typed in the free-text "Describe it" field.
- **`InlineWizard.tsx`** and **`TemplatePickerModal.tsx`**: neither has any stage, toggle, or field for "how many pages" / "which pages do you want." The Features stage (`lib/features.ts`) offers things like contact forms, records, service areas, etc., but nothing about page structure.
- So a customer who types "I want a Home, About, Services, and Contact page" into the wizard's Describe box gets that text appended *after* a hardcoded "Build a one-page website..." opener — actively contradicting their own request rather than staying silent on it. Their only real path to multi-page is: (a) skip the wizard/templates entirely, write a free-form prompt themselves that clearly asks for pages, or (b) get lucky that the model interprets "and a Services and Contact page" strongly enough to override the "one-page" framing that its own stitched-together brief just told it.

This is a genuine, specific UI/prompt-assembly gap, not just "under-explained" — the customer-facing paths actively push toward one-page by default and never surface the capability that clearly exists server-side.

**6. Edit-turn robustness / orphan risk**

- The build pipeline fully regenerates `kind: "build"` rows every publish (`deleteMany` then `createMany` from the fresh `vite build` output — `app/api/generate/route.ts` ~line 339), so the *served* tree can never contain a build artifact for a page whose `.html` source no longer exists. That part is safe.
- However, `kind: "source"` files are only touched by whatever `write_file`/`delete_file` calls the model actually makes (`onWrite`/`onDelete` in `app/api/generate/route.ts`, ~lines 263–282) — there is no code-level referential-integrity check between `src/pages.tsx`'s table and the set of `.html` shells, or between `pages.tsx` and `src/pages/*.tsx` component files.
- Two concrete failure modes are possible, and nothing in code prevents them, only the prompt's care in following its own (page-adding-only) instructions:
  - Model removes a page's `pages.tsx` entry but forgets to `delete_file` the `.html` shell → `vite.config.ts`'s scanner still finds the `.html` file (it scans disk, not `pages.tsx`), so the page keeps building, keeps appearing in `sitemap.xml`, and stays reachable at its URL — orphaned/zombie page, invisible in nav but live and indexed.
  - Model deletes the `.html` shell but forgets to remove the `pages.tsx`/`SiteNav` entry → the nav renders a link to a page whose file no longer exists, and clicking it produces a real 404 (the route deliberately doesn't SPA-fallback).
- No tests exercise this specific scenario (`tests/site-seo.test.mjs` and `tests/build-diff.test.mjs` cover SEO correctness and the diff-viewer's line math, not page-table/file-tree consistency across an edit turn). No comments in the codebase acknowledge this as a known/tracked issue.
- This risk is mitigated somewhat by edit turns receiving the *entire* current file tree as context (`describeFiles()` in `lib/agent.ts`), so a capable model *can* see and fix all three places — but it's relying on the model's general competence and the "change only what the request calls for" instruction, not on an explicit "how to retire a page" checklist the way adding a page gets one.

## Assessment

**The underlying engineering is solid.** Router, page table, per-page `.html` shells + Vite auto-discovery, per-page canonical/OG tags, and sitemap generation are all well-designed, mutually consistent, and covered by real tests for the SEO-correctness half. This is not a fragile edge case bolted on — `vite.config.ts`'s comment block and `site-seo.ts`'s comment block both show deliberate design work specifically for the multi-page case (e.g., the canonical-URL bug this was designed to avoid is explicitly tested against). Nested paths, arbitrary depth, and multiple pages sharing one bundle all work correctly end-to-end for a **single build turn**.

**Two real, distinct problems remain, and they are different in kind:**

1. **A genuine UI/UX gap (needs product/copy work, not backend engineering)**: the customer-facing wizard and template gallery actively steer toward one-page sites — every template and the generic wizard skeleton hardcode "Build a one-page website" as the literal opening instruction sent to the model, and there is no field or toggle anywhere for a customer to say "I want these pages." A customer has no discoverable way to ask for multi-page short of writing a fully custom prompt and hoping their multi-page language overrides the wizard's own "one-page" framing. This is squarely "under-surfaced" — the capability is real, but the funnel actively hides/contradicts it.

2. **A real (if narrower) functional gap in edit-turn reliability (needs engineering)**: removing/renaming a page depends entirely on the model correctly touching three separate files (page component, `pages.tsx` entry, `.html` shell) with no explicit "how to retire a page" prompt guidance and no code-level consistency check. This can silently produce either an orphaned page (still built, still indexed, invisible in nav) or a broken nav link (404). Fixing this well would mean either: (a) adding explicit removal guidance to the `lib/agent.ts` prompt (cheap, quick win), and/or (b) a lightweight server-side consistency check after an edit turn (e.g., warn or auto-clean when a `.html` file exists with no `pages.tsx` entry, or vice versa) — a real, scoped piece of engineering work.

In short: don't rebuild the plumbing — it's good. Do (a) fix the wizard/template funnel so a customer can actually ask for multi-page cleanly, and (b) close the edit-turn consistency gap around page removal, ideally with both a prompt fix and a small backend safety net.
